new_statements.rule_in_words: Cone (Nyinpa variety) has a two-toneme system, high vs low, contrastive on the word-initial syllable; the tone of a non-initial syllable is predictable (a high first syllable spreads H rightward, HL > HH, in compounds; after a low first syllable the second is high if its vowel is short, and if long it is high after a voiceless obstruent onset and low/rising after a voiced onset, with free variation). Tone is neutralized on aspirated-onset syllables (low with a long vowel, high with a short one; high-in-isolation aspirated syllables become low when suffixed). The words 'stress' and 'prominence' (as an accentual notion) do not occur; the only 'accent' is the grave-accent diacritic marking extra-low case suffixes (p. 43). No word-stress placement is stated and stress is neither asserted nor denied.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; no stress of any kind is discussed.
new_statements.exceptions: Case markers and some verbal suffixes are always realized low and block rightward H spread (pp. 7, 43); tone not contrastive after aspirated onsets (p. 7); long-vowel second syllables with voiced onsets vary freely between H and L (p. 7); a handful of lexical exceptions to the tonogenesis rules are tabulated in section 3.1 (p. 9), where Jacques also notes that Qu (1962)'s variety assigns high tone to some syllables that are low in Nyinpa.
new_statements.identity_note: Jacques describes the Nyinpa village (Niba 尼巴, Chas.bu gshus / Cheba gou valley, southwest Cone/Zhuoni county, Gannan, Gansu) variety, from one 23-year-old consultant recorded in Chengdu in 2010; he states that the tonal system 'slightly differs from the variety of Cone Tibetan described by Qu (1962)' (preprint p. 9).

tone_statements.quote: 本稿で扱う sDedgu dgon 方言では、２節に示したように、調値による声調を認めない。一方で、母音の短さと発声類型による記述を提案し、理論的には、その組み合わせで計４種の超分節音的対立を形成することができるとする。... sDedgu dgon 方言のレジスターの対立は、高低レジスターの差異として記述する。レジスターは、その音声学的性質上、音節を単位として現れるが、語頭で弁別的に働くと解釈できる。... レジスターは、聴覚印象としては、発声類型よりもピッチに特徴づけられる。高レジスターが有標であり、ピッチが高めに指定され、場合によって声門の緊張が高くなる。... いずれにおいても、ピッチの相対的な高さの違いだけでは弁別に寄与しない。
tone_statements.translation: In the sDedgu dgon dialect treated here, as shown in section 2, tone defined by pitch values is not recognised. Instead a description by vowel shortness and phonation type is proposed; in theory their combination can form four suprasegmental oppositions. ... The register opposition of the sDedgu dgon dialect is described as a difference between high and low register. By its phonetic nature register appears with the syllable as its unit, but it can be interpreted as working distinctively at the beginning of the word. ... As an auditory impression, register is characterised by pitch rather than by phonation type. High register is the marked term: pitch is specified as relatively high and in some cases glottal tension increases. ... In either case, a difference in relative pitch height alone does not contribute to the distinction.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote verified verbatim at the stated locator in the HAL v2 PDF we hold/text (sec. 2.3, printed pp. 6-8). (2) The deciding source is a specialist's full phonological profile (preprint of the 2014 Academia Sinica chapter that Glottolog ranks first for this languoid); no better or instrumental description of Cone prosody exists per Glottolog and web search. (3) Three open sources downloaded now on another Cone dialect (Bragkhoglung: Suzuki 2012 p.3, Suzuki 2017 p.45, Zou & Suzuki 2022 pp.4-5) all describe a two-way word-tone (pitch) system with the contrast located at the word onset and say nothing of stress -- matching our 'tonal, H vs L contrastive on the first syllable, non-initial tones predictable' coding. (4) Only upgrade available is bibliographic: add the published Jacques 2014 citation alongside the preprint; no reclassification.

sources.quote: (Japanese) 'Two tones are recognised, each bearing on the word as a unit: high word-onset vs low word-onset. Only the pitch of the word onset is distinctive; whether there is a fall toward syllable/word end is not distinctive, and polysyllabic words usually show a falling intonation.' Also notes (fn. 9, p. 12) that rNam-rgyal Tshe-brtan (2008) gives no consistent description of tone. No stress/accent described.

sources.note: Rejects a contour/pitch-value tone analysis for sDedgu dgon (contrasting with Renzeng Wangmu 2013's five tones 55/51/54/35/12 for Rongdwangs); posits two suprasegmental distinctions: a high vs low REGISTER (high marked, higher pitch, sometimes glottal tension; distinctive on the word-initial syllable) and an independent extra-short vowel feature (falling or high-level pitch) corresponding to Written Tibetan open syllables; no minimal pairs by register alone; no word-stress statement.

sources.note: Abstract read online: 'In these languages, it is only Cone which has a pitch distinction in its phonology. On the other hand, mBrugchu has no suprasegmentals which function in the phonology but it has a phonetically clear realisation of breathy voice'; proposes 'registrogenesis' (phonation-based registers preceding pitch), ordering mBrugchu (most phonation-like) > dPalskyid, Khodpokhog > Thewo, Sharkhog, Khromjekhog > Cone (most pitch-like).
